full_script: When you look at an apple, you see red. A computer, however, only understands numbers. To bridge this gap between our colorful reality and a machine's mathematical brain, we break images down into tiny, illuminated building blocks called pixels. How does a pixel know what color to be? It uses the RGB color model, which mimics the biology of human vision. Every pixel contains three sub-pixels: Red, Green, and Blue. By mixing different intensities of these three lights, screens can trick your brain into seeing almost any color imaginable. To precisely measure the intensity of each sub-pixel, computers use a system called bit depth. Standard color imaging uses an 8-bit system for each of the three channels. Mathematically, this means two to the eighth power, resulting in 256 possible combinations per channel. Because a computer starts counting at zero, this gives us a range from 0 to 255. Zero means the light is completely off, and 255 means the light is at maximum brightness. These values act as mathematical coordinates for color. Pure red is (255, 0, 0). If you turn all the lights off to (0, 0, 0), you get pitch black. Turn them all the way up to 255, and you get a blinding white. To find the total number of colors a standard monitor can display, we multiply the 256 levels of each channel together. 256 times 256 times 256 equals 16,777,216. That is nearly 16.8 million unique colors, with every single one mapped to a specific mathematical coordinate. The next time you look at a stunning digital photograph, remember what you are really seeing. You aren't seeing the sunset. You are seeing millions of microscopic lights, executing billions of mathematical calculations every second, perfectly orchestrated to replicate the beauty of the real world.
